book.author: Shane Parrish

chapters.title: The Map Is Not the Territory
chapters.hook: The green dashboard looks calm until one live customer call starts ringing through the room.
chapters.counterintuition: A clean map can make you less aware, not more; but the better move is to use the map as a shortcut, then let the territory interrupt it before the shortcut becomes command.
chapters.tryThisNow: Choose a trusted report. Before acting, write one direct territory check: a call to make, a work sample to inspect, or a room to walk.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Use maps because reality is too large to carry, but keep testing the map against the territory before it starts ruling the decision.

breakdown.fastRead:
Tinny hold music fills the conference room. The dashboard says customer wait time is fine. The complaint log says callers are furious. Hannah does not debate which signal deserves respect. She puts the support line on speakerphone and lets the timer run past the promised answer time.

That is the move. A map is a reduction of the territory, not the territory itself. Metrics, resumes, plans, and reports help because they leave things out. They harm when the missing parts stop feeling missing.

Use the map, then touch the ground.
breakdown.deepRead:
A dashboard said the line was moving; Jeff Bezos picked up the phone and let the customer line answer back. That story matters because the problem was not the existence of a metric. The problem was that the metric had become easier to trust than the people it claimed to represent.

Every useful map is incomplete on purpose. A financial statement cannot carry every invoice, customer argument, supplier delay, and shelf of unsold stock. A resume cannot show whether a candidate can keep their hands steady at the bench. A policy cannot hold every exception a real hallway will produce. The reduction is what makes the tool usable. It is also what makes overconfidence possible.

The test is contact.

Newton and Einstein make the point cleanly: one map can work across much of the terrain while another shows where the terrain changes under its feet. That is the mature way to treat models. Do not worship them, and do not throw them away the first time they show an edge. Ask where the map works, what it leaves out, and what kind of evidence would force an update.

The limit is important. Anecdotes are not automatically superior to data. A complaint can be noisy, selective, or wrong. The discipline is to make the map answer to the territory, not to replace one blind faith with another.
breakdown.fullRead:
Michael stands at the river tailgate with a laminated habitat map and six muddy boot photos. The grant plan points to the north bend. The boot photos point to the south bank, where the saplings are actually failing. If he treats the map as the decision, money moves cleanly and wrongly. If he treats the map as a question, the next step is obvious: reconcile the picture with the ground before the purchase order goes out.

That is why the cartographer matters. A map carries the maker's purpose. A call-center dashboard may count average answer time because that number is easy to collect. A resume may reward polish because polish is easy to read. A city plan may favor straight lines because straight lines are easy to defend in a meeting. The map is not lying. It is choosing.

What has your current map chosen to ignore?

Jane Jacobs matters because the plan did not merely describe the city; it tried to make the city obey the drawing. That is the deeper danger. Once a map gets power, people begin serving it. Students serve the ranking. Teams serve the status report. Managers serve the green tile. A representation can start shaping the territory it was meant to describe.

Rachel sees the smaller version at the apprenticeship bench. One resume is perfect. The other is uneven, patched together from odd jobs and a short certificate. The map says the polished candidate is safer. Then the caliper test begins. Five minutes later, the messy resume is attached to steadier hands. The right lesson is not to ignore resumes. It is to remember what they are: compressed guesses about work that still needs to be watched.

Maps earn trust by staying connected. They lose trust when they become easier to defend than reality. That can happen slowly. A metric looks useful, then official, then sacred. A plan starts as coordination, then becomes a reason to stop seeing the room. A review form begins as a memory aid, then turns into the only thing anyone is allowed to notice.

Use the abstraction. Inspect the maker. Check the ground. The order matters because a clean abstraction can make a bad decision feel tidy. When the stakes rise, add one direct contact point: a call, a sample, a walk-through, a field photo, or a complaint read in full. That contact point does not replace the map. It keeps the map answerable.

Use the abstraction. Inspect the maker. Check the ground. Watch for the moment the scorecard starts rewriting the game.

The point is not suspicion for its own sake. You cannot run a hospital, shop, classroom, or software service by direct inspection of everything. You need reductions. The skill is knowing when the reduction has gathered too much authority. High stakes, strong incentives, strange complaints, and signals that look too smooth are all reasons to go touch the territory.

A map that still answers to the ground is leverage. A map that refuses correction is a trap with clean labels.

examples.title: Claire Lets the Hold Music Run
examples.scenario: Tinny hold music fills the glass conference room before anyone says the word metric. Claire, the operations lead, has the green dashboard tile open beside a customer complaint log full of missed renewal calls. The report promises answers in under a minute. The speakerphone timer crosses ninety seconds while the executives stare at it. Claire has to decide before the renewal review ends whether the dashboard still gets to govern the staffing call.
examples.whatToDo: Let the call keep running, write the actual wait time beside the green tile, and pause the staffing decision until the metric explains the customer experience it claims to measure.
examples.whyItMatters: The live call is the territory pushing back. It does not make the dashboard useless; it shows the edge where the reduction stopped matching the thing it was built to track.

examples.title: Michael Delays the Grant Order
examples.scenario: The tailgate is wet with boot grit and a laminated habitat map curls at the corners. Michael, a conservation coordinator, sets the map beside six muddy photos from this morning's river walk. The grant order points to the north bend. The photos show saplings failing on the south bank. His pen hovers over the purchase request, and he must decide whether the map is enough or the field evidence gets another visit.
examples.whatToDo: Stop the purchase request, mark the disagreement between the map and the photos, and send the crew back to the river before committing the grant money.
examples.whyItMatters: The map is useful for narrowing attention, not for ending inspection. When the field photos disagree, the next action has to reconnect the plan to the ground.

examples.title: Rachel Watches the Caliper Test
examples.scenario: It took Rachel one minute to prefer the perfect resume and five minutes to doubt it. The caliper blinks on the tool-room bench beside two applications. One candidate's paper looks tidy; the other reads like a patchwork of odd jobs. Rachel predicts the polished candidate will finish first, then watches the uneven resume solve the setup cleanly. She must decide which map of skill deserves the offer.
examples.whatToDo: Treat the resume as a first filter, not a verdict. Put the bench test result beside the paper record and hire from the work that actually showed up.
examples.whyItMatters: A resume is a compressed story about ability. The bench test brings the territory into the room, where neat paper can lose to steadier hands.

examples.title: Olivier Marks the Desire Paths
examples.scenario: You stand by the mulch while chalk arrows cross the future swing area. Olivier, the parks planner, follows parents with a clipboard and marks where strollers actually turn. The approved plan keeps every path clean and square. The ground keeps drawing diagonals. Before the contractor stakes the first post, Olivier must decide whether the safety diagram is describing movement or trying to command it.
examples.whatToDo: Move the plan back into contact with the site. Add the desire paths to the drawing before the layout hardens into concrete, fencing, and frustrated families.
examples.whyItMatters: The approved plan has authority, but the walking paths reveal behavior. If the design ignores the territory, families will either resist it or be shaped badly by it.

examples.title: Aman Writes in the Missing Vendors
examples.scenario: Which number belongs in the fee vote: vendor revenue or the empty end stalls after closing? Aman, the market treasurer, folds two stall weights where vegetable tents used to stand and carries them to the office. The vendor-revenue sheet looks strong because the largest booths are paying more. He writes the missing small vendors in the margin before next Saturday's board packet is printed.
examples.whatToDo: Add the absence to the sheet. Count the vendors the revenue map has erased before voting on a fee increase that may keep the spreadsheet healthy and weaken the market.
examples.whyItMatters: A map can hide losses by counting what remains. The empty stalls are not sentimental detail; they are part of the territory the decision will change.

examples.title: Marit Rewrites the Incident Definition
examples.scenario: "The site was up," someone says, while a customer's screen recording shows a frozen login spinner for forty-two seconds. Marit, the reliability lead, has the uptime report on one monitor and the incident log on the other. Before the weekly report goes out, she changes the incident definition so degraded login failures count as failures, not footnotes.
examples.whatToDo: Revise the map so it tracks the experience that matters. Keep uptime, but add degraded login failure to the incident definition before the report earns another green week.
examples.whyItMatters: The old metric was technically true and practically misleading. Better definitions keep the representation attached to what customers are actually trying to do.

questions.prompt: A support team has a dashboard showing healthy response times, but three large customers send recordings of long waits. What is the first disciplined move?
choices: Treat the recordings as complaints that can be reviewed after the dashboard trend changes.
Run a direct check of the support line and compare the actual wait with the dashboard's definition.
Replace the dashboard with customer anecdotes because direct stories are always more reliable.
questions.explanation: The direct check makes the map answer to the territory. The recordings should not be dismissed, but replacing measurement with anecdotes repeats the same overtrust problem in another form.

questions.prompt: A hiring panel has two candidates: one perfect resume, one uneven resume with a strong work sample. Which action best fits the map-territory move?
choices: Use the resume as a filter, then let the work sample revise the panel's confidence.
Ignore the resume entirely because paper credentials are only a map.
Choose the polished resume because it is easier to defend if the hire fails.
questions.explanation: The resume remains useful as a reduction, but the work sample is closer to the territory. Ignoring paper completely or choosing defensibility both confuse convenience with evidence.

questions.prompt: A city planner has a clean park diagram, but parents keep walking across a muddy diagonal path. Which response shows the strongest judgment?
choices: Keep the diagram because plans need consistency once approved.
Ask whether the informal path reveals movement the approved plan failed to capture.
Remove the diagonal path quickly so visitors learn the official route.
questions.explanation: The muddy path is territory evidence. It may not automatically decide the design, but it should force the planner to question what the diagram omitted before the plan hardens.

questions.prompt: A nonprofit scorecard rewards the number of people served, and staff begin choosing easier cases to keep the number high. What has happened?
choices: The staff have proved that measurement should be removed from the nonprofit.
The scorecard has started influencing the territory it was meant to describe.
The original service goal was probably too difficult to measure accurately.
questions.explanation: The map is no longer passive. The score changes staff behavior, so the organization must inspect the incentive the metric created rather than simply trust the clean count.

questions.prompt: A clinic policy says patients receive discharge instructions, but nurses report that confused patients keep calling the next day. Which move best tests the policy?
choices: Review whether the policy was signed by the correct committee.
Watch one discharge conversation and call one patient the next morning to see what they understood.
Send a reminder email telling nurses to follow the policy more carefully.
questions.explanation: The policy is a map of intended practice. Watching the conversation and checking patient understanding tests whether the map still touches what happens in the hallway and at home.

questions.prompt: An executive says a customer-satisfaction average proves a launch is working. The comments are polarized: some love it, many cannot finish setup. What should an analyst notice?
choices: The average may be compressing the territory in a way that hides a failure mode.
The comments are emotional and should not update a numerical metric.
The average is invalid because all summaries conceal some detail.
questions.explanation: Averages reduce reality. That reduction can be useful, but here it may hide a setup failure. The answer is not to worship comments or reject summaries outright.

questions.prompt: A school ranking pushes teachers to spend less time with students who need slow help because quick improvements lift the score. Which diagnosis is most precise?
choices: The ranking is a bad map because schools cannot be compared.
The ranking is useful only if every classroom uses the same curriculum.
The map has become a target, and the territory is changing to flatter the score.
questions.explanation: The ranking is now shaping behavior. Whether comparison is possible is a separate issue; the immediate danger is that people are optimizing the proxy instead of the learning.

questions.prompt: A warehouse manager trusts a safety checklist, but workers keep moving around one blind corner without scanning badges. Which action best uses the map without worshiping it?
choices: Stand at the corner during shift change and compare actual movement with the checklist step.
Add a second signature line to the checklist so workers take it seriously.
Remove the checklist because observed behavior is the only thing that counts.
questions.explanation: The corner observation tests the checklist against the territory. More signatures may only strengthen the map, and removing the checklist loses a tool that may still help once corrected.

questions.prompt: A hospital dashboard, patient interviews, and direct hallway observation all disagree about discharge delays. Which plan is best?
choices: Follow the dashboard because it is the only consistent source.
Follow the interviews because lived experience outranks all reports.
Map what each source measures, then use direct observation to find where the representation breaks.
questions.explanation: The strongest plan keeps multiple maps in play and checks their range against the ground. Choosing one source as sacred, even interviews, skips the work of locating the mismatch.

reviewCards.front: A report looks clean, but the people closest to the work keep objecting. What should you retrieve?
reviewCards.back: A map is a reduction of the territory. Use the report, but test it against one direct contact point before letting it govern the choice.

reviewCards.front: A metric has become the target people optimize. What danger should you name?
reviewCards.back: The map may be influencing the territory. Once rewards attach to a proxy, people can start serving the proxy instead of the reality it was meant to track.

reviewCards.front: A resume and a work sample point in different directions. Which one is closer to the territory?
reviewCards.back: The work sample is closer to the actual ability being judged. The resume is still useful, but it should lose authority when the work itself gives better evidence.

reviewCards.front: A model has worked for years, then fails in one edge case. What should you remember?
reviewCards.back: A useful map can still have a range. The right move is to find the edge, update the model, and keep using it where it still earns trust.

reviewCards.front: Before trusting a map made by someone else, what question protects you?
reviewCards.back: Ask what the cartographer chose to count, ignore, and reward. Those choices shape what the map can show and what it will quietly hide.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: You learn to keep representations useful without letting them become sovereign. The skill is simple: name the map, inspect what it omits, and run one direct territory check when stakes or strange signals rise.

ifThenPlans.plan: If a dashboard will decide staffing, budget, or priority, then pair it with one live customer, worker, or process check before the decision is final.
If a resume makes a candidate look obviously safe, then require one work sample that tests the actual skill the role needs.
If a plan looks elegant on paper, then walk the place or process it describes and mark one behavior the plan did not show.
If a story about yourself feels clean and settled, then ask what recent behavior or result would complicate that story.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Before your next decision based on a report, plan, score, or summary, perform one territory check: call one person, inspect one work sample, observe one process, or walk one place.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Each Friday, choose one map that guided your week. Write what it helped you see, what it may have hidden, who made it, and one change you would make before trusting it again.

chapters.title: Circle of Competence
chapters.hook: The cheese room smells profitable; the refrigerated shipping quote belongs to a different game.
chapters.counterintuition: Competence is not the same as transferable advantage, but confidence often keeps walking after the earned edge ends.
chapters.tryThisNow: Pick one live decision and draw three boxes: play, learn, defer. Put each part of the decision where your earned evidence says it belongs.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Your circle of competence protects judgment only when you know the perimeter and treat nearby unfamiliar games as places to learn or defer.

breakdown.fastRead:
The cheese room smells sharp and profitable. Andrew knows the suppliers, the aging racks, and the customers who ask for washed rind by name. Then he opens a refrigerated meal-kit shipping quote and feels the old confidence arrive in a new room.

That is where the circle of competence gets tested. Inside the circle, you have earned knowledge. Near the perimeter, the edge thins. Outside it, someone else understands the game better than you do.

The goal is not to stay small. It is to stop pretending the edge moved just because your confidence did.
breakdown.deepRead:
Rose Blumkin's edge was not a halo around every business problem; it was furniture, cash, leases, and the ground she knew by touch. She could read that territory because she had spent years paying attention to it. That kind of competence has weight.

The trouble starts when weight in one place feels like weight everywhere. Even a chess grandmaster can see sixty-four squares clearly and still be a beginner when the board changes. Pattern recognition travels badly when the feedback, incentives, and hidden rules are different.

Perimeter is the whole skill when confidence travels.

Sophie faces it in the triage bay. Blue gel dries around the ultrasound probe while a resident asks for a fast read. She knows the bedside protocol, the patient's pain score, and the moment to call radiology. She does not know enough to replace the radiologist. Her competence is real precisely because she can name where it ends.

This is what makes the model more demanding than a comfort-zone slogan. The honest perimeter may tell you to play, but it may also tell you to study, ask for help, or make a small test while feedback is still cheap.

The limit matters. A circle of competence is not an excuse to avoid learning. You can expand it by doing the work, getting feedback, and paying the price of being new. What breaks judgment is claiming the expanded circle before the evidence is there.
breakdown.fullRead:
Nicolas is brilliant at the chess club. He can look at a position and feel the weak square before the teenagers finish writing down the move. Then a poker stream invites him to join a charity table. The river card glows on his laptop. A wooden chess clock sits beside it like a false passport. He reviews one hand aloud, hears himself speaking with chess certainty, and stops.

The hand is not a position. The players are not pieces. Hidden cards, betting pressure, bankroll, and bluffing change the game. Nicolas can learn poker, but he cannot import mastery whole. The honest label for the invitation is learn, not play.

Where are you borrowing confidence from a nearby room?

Charlie Munger's warning is blunt: the other table may look open, but it belongs to people who have paid for knowledge you are only borrowing. That is not fear. It is respect for earned advantage. Inside the circle, you can see distinctions others miss. Outside it, the distinctions are still there, but they belong to someone else.

Mikkel sees the same thing on a loading dock. The neighboring building looks like a warehouse decision. He knows racks, forklifts, lease rates, and winter heating bills. Then he unfolds the zoning packet under a tape measure and sees a fight he has never learned to read. The competent move is not to walk away automatically. It is to circle the lease terms he understands, slide the zoning packet to counsel, and keep the signature page still.

The false pride version says, I have succeeded before, so I can trust myself here. The timid version says, I should never step outside my lane. Both miss the point. The circle is a map of earned reliability, not a prison. You can enter a new area as a student. You can partner with someone whose edge covers your gap. You can place a small bet while feedback is cheap. What you cannot do safely is call borrowed certainty competence.

Layla learns this in a rights contract. She can cut a documentary until the story breathes. She cannot explain three international distribution clauses without guessing. The festival lanyard on the table belongs to her world. The redlined rights language does not. Once she highlights the clauses she can defend and the clauses a lawyer must read, the decision gets cleaner.

The circle also gives you a constructive path outward. If Nicolas wants poker competence, he can study hand histories, play tiny stakes, and measure feedback before the charity table. If Mikkel wants zoning judgment, he can learn the code with counsel while keeping the purchase unsigned. The boundary is not a wall; it is a label on the price of learning.

The circle protects you by lowering the volume on false confidence. It asks a practical question before every serious choice: where do I have an earned edge, where am I learning, and where should someone better informed take the lead?

Play where the edge is real. Learn where the gap is honest. Defer before confidence starts spending money it did not earn.

examples.title: Andrew Marks the Guess Column
examples.scenario: The ammoniac bite of washed-rind cheese hangs in the prep room while Andrew lays his aged-cheese margin sheet beside a refrigerated meal-kit shipping quote. He knows local suppliers and Saturday customers cold. He does not know spoilage rates across three provinces. His thumb rests on the approval email, and he has to decide whether this is still his game or a nearby game with different rules. He writes spoilage rate, packing labor, and failed-delivery refunds in the guess column before anyone orders new packaging.
examples.whatToDo: Mark each line as earned knowledge or guesswork before approving the expansion. Play the cheese-margin game, but learn or partner on refrigerated shipping.
examples.whyItMatters: Competence lives in particulars. Knowing aging rooms and customers gives Andrew an edge, but cold-chain logistics can transfer that edge to people who have earned a different map.

examples.title: Sophie Names the Radiology Edge
examples.scenario: "Can you tell if that's fluid?" the resident asks while blue gel dries around the ultrasound probe in triage bay three. Sophie, the senior nurse, checks the bedside protocol and the radiology callback time. "I can verify placement and pain response," she says. "I cannot read the scan." Before the dose is changed, she must tell the team where her edge ends. The resident still gets speed, but not a pretend interpretation outside Sophie's feedback history.
examples.whatToDo: State the competent part out loud, then hand off the interpretation. Keep the protocol moving without pretending a nearby clinical skill is yours.
examples.whyItMatters: The patient needs speed and accuracy. Sophie's competence helps only while it stays inside the boundary where her training and feedback are real.

examples.title: Nicolas Writes Learn Beside the Invite
examples.scenario: Which game is Nicolas actually good at? The paused river card glows on his laptop beside a wooden chess clock. The charity stream invitation includes a fee and a public table. Nicolas reviews one hand aloud, predicts the obvious fold, then hears two players explain pot odds he never considered. He must decide whether his chess pattern skill is an edge here or only borrowed confidence. The public table can wait until he has real poker feedback instead of familiar confidence.
examples.whatToDo: Write learn beside the invitation, not play. Treat poker as a new feedback system, even if the pattern-recognition feeling is familiar.
examples.whyItMatters: A nearby game can feel like home while hiding different rules. The perimeter protects Nicolas from mistaking one kind of expertise for another.

examples.title: Mikkel Slides the Zoning Packet
examples.scenario: It took Mikkel three pages to stop treating the neighboring building as a warehouse problem. A folded zoning packet lies under a tape measure on the loading dock, next to his lease ledger. He circles freight access, heating cost, and rack layout in blue. Then he slides the zoning packet across the desk to counsel. Before the purchase meeting, he must decide which parts he knows and which parts only look familiar.
examples.whatToDo: Split the deal by competence. Keep the lease and operations judgments, but move the zoning fight to someone whose edge covers that terrain.
examples.whyItMatters: The familiar building can hide an unfamiliar rule system. Naming the perimeter keeps Mikkel's warehouse knowledge useful without letting it overrun legal risk.

examples.title: Layla Highlights the Clauses She Cannot Defend
examples.scenario: You watch Layla at the editing suite table, a festival lanyard lying across a redlined rights contract. She can explain every cut in the documentary and almost none of the international distribution language. After one bad clause nearly locks the film away from festivals, she marks what she can defend unaided and what needs a distribution lawyer before any future signature page moves.
examples.whatToDo: Separate creative competence from rights competence. Highlight the clauses that exceed Layla's earned knowledge and get expert review before signing.
examples.whyItMatters: A finished film does not make its creator competent in every contract attached to it. The circle preserves the work by admitting where another edge is needed.

examples.title: Janek Asks Where His Home Range Ends
examples.scenario: Wind-slab crystals skitter across a tailgate map outside the guide hut. Janek has twenty seasons of route feel in his home range, but this valley's avalanche bulletin reads differently. The local forecaster points to a loaded slope his eye had treated as harmless. Janek writes the day's route only after asking which parts of his home judgment do not transfer here. The ski team gets a weather handoff from the person who reads that mountain every morning.
examples.whatToDo: Use the home-range skill as a starting point, then ask the local forecaster where it fails. Build the route around the edge of Janek's knowledge.
examples.whyItMatters: Confidence can travel faster than competence in the mountains. The snowpack does not care where Janek earned his instincts; it tests only whether they apply here.

questions.prompt: A bakery owner understands recipes, local demand, and suppliers, but wants to launch frozen national shipping. What should she identify first?
choices: Whether frozen shipping is inside earned competence, a learn zone, or a defer zone.
Whether her current customers would praise the idea.
Whether a competitor has already made the same move.
questions.explanation: The first issue is perimeter. Current bakery skill may not cover cold-chain shipping. Customer praise and competitor behavior can help later, but they do not prove competence.

questions.prompt: A respected surgeon is asked to advise on hospital cybersecurity because she leads well under pressure. Which response best fits the model?
choices: Accept, because pressure judgment transfers across serious domains.
Define the leadership help she can give and defer the technical security assessment to specialists.
Decline every part of the request because the topic is outside her original training.
questions.explanation: Leadership may be inside her circle, while technical security is not. The right move splits the request rather than pretending all skill transfers or refusing useful help.

questions.prompt: At a charity poker stream, a chess coach sees the river card glow beside his wooden chess clock and says, I read patterns for a living. What is the strongest warning before he pays the buy-in?
choices: Poker is mostly luck, so expertise cannot matter.
Chess expertise may create overconfidence because the hidden rules and feedback are different.
He should play only if the buy-in is small enough to lose.
questions.explanation: The warning is transfer error. Chess pattern skill is real, but poker has different information, incentives, and feedback. A smaller buy-in manages loss but does not create competence.

questions.prompt: A restaurant manager knows front-of-house flow and wants to renegotiate the building's tax assessment alone. Which action is soundest?
choices: Handle it alone because long experience in the building provides enough context.
Avoid the issue because property assessment is outside the restaurant business.
Name what building facts he knows and bring in someone with assessment expertise for the rest.
questions.explanation: The strongest move preserves real knowledge while deferring the unfamiliar assessment game. Experience with the building does not automatically cover the legal and valuation rules.

questions.prompt: A designer has built successful mobile apps and now wants to price enterprise software contracts. What question should come before confidence?
choices: Which parts of pricing have I learned through direct feedback, and which parts am I guessing?
How quickly can I learn the new pricing vocabulary?
Which previous app launch felt most similar to this contract?
questions.explanation: The question separates earned knowledge from guesses. Vocabulary and analogy can help learning, but neither proves that enterprise pricing is inside the current circle.

questions.prompt: A mountain guide from one range arrives in a new valley and feels confident reading the slopes. The local bulletin warns about a pattern he rarely sees. What should he do?
choices: Trust his years of field instinct because snow knowledge is snow knowledge.
Cancel the trip because any unfamiliar pattern means the whole day is unknowable.
Ask where his home-range judgment stops applying and build the route around the local warning.
questions.explanation: The years of skill matter, but the perimeter has moved. The bulletin and local knowledge show where his advantage thins, so the route must respect that edge.

questions.prompt: A filmmaker understands editing and story but cannot explain several distribution clauses. Which behavior best shows competence rather than insecurity?
choices: Highlight the unknown clauses and get a distribution lawyer before signing.
Sign because business details should not slow a finished creative project.
Reject the whole contract because unfamiliar clauses are always traps.
questions.explanation: Competence includes knowing its edge. The lawyer does not replace Layla's creative judgment; the lawyer covers a different game attached to the work.

questions.prompt: A software founder succeeded in consumer subscriptions and assumes she can price a hospital procurement bid. What is the likely failure mode?
choices: She is confusing courage with competence because all new markets require boldness.
She is letting real success in one feedback system masquerade as edge in another.
She is overvaluing expertise because procurement rules can be learned from public documents.
questions.explanation: The danger is misplaced transfer. Consumer subscriptions and hospital procurement can look adjacent while using different buyers, timelines, incentives, and failure costs.

questions.prompt: A regional retailer can expand into a nearby product line alone, partner with an expert, or run a small learning pilot. Which choice best reflects the circle of competence?
choices: Expand alone if the new product reaches the same customers.
Avoid the expansion until the team has full mastery.
Choose among play, partner, and pilot based on which parts are earned knowledge and which are not.
questions.explanation: The model does not force avoidance. It asks for an accurate perimeter, then matches the action to it: play where edge is real, partner or pilot where learning is still owed.

reviewCards.front: You feel confident in a decision near your usual work. What should you retrieve before acting?
reviewCards.back: Confidence may have crossed the perimeter before competence did. Name what you know from earned feedback and what only feels familiar.

reviewCards.front: A skill worked in one domain and you want to use it in another. What is the transfer test?
reviewCards.back: Ask whether the feedback, incentives, hidden rules, and failure costs are the same. If they changed, your circle may not have moved with your confidence.

reviewCards.front: A problem has three parts: one you know, one you can learn cheaply, and one with high stakes. How do you sort them?
reviewCards.back: Play where the edge is earned, learn where feedback is cheap, and defer where another person clearly understands the game better.

reviewCards.front: Why is knowing the perimeter often more important than having a large circle?
reviewCards.back: A small circle with a clear edge protects decisions. A large-feeling circle with a fuzzy edge invites expensive pretending when the advantage has already transferred to someone else.

reviewCards.front: How can you expand the circle without pretending it has already expanded?
reviewCards.back: Enter as a learner: make small bets, seek feedback, partner with people who have the edge, and wait for evidence before upgrading confidence into competence.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: You learn to sort decisions by earned edge. The skill is not retreating from unfamiliar work; it is naming whether you should play, learn, partner, or defer before confidence starts spending money.

ifThenPlans.plan: If a new project feels adjacent to work you know, then list the rules, feedback loops, and failure costs that may be different before committing.
If someone asks for advice outside your edge, then say what you can judge and name the specialist needed for the rest.
If an opportunity sounds clear after one explanation, then write whether you understand the mechanics or only the story.
If you want to expand into a new area, then choose a small feedback-rich pilot before taking a full-sized risk.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Choose one pending decision and mark each part as play, learn, partner, or defer. Take one action that matches the weakest label, not the strongest feeling.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once a week, review a decision where you felt confident. Write what evidence proved the confidence was earned, where the perimeter was unclear, and what feedback would expand the circle next time.

memorableLines.text: The goal is not to stay small. It is to stop pretending the edge moved just because your confidence did.
Perimeter is the whole skill when confidence travels.
Play where the edge is real. Learn where the gap is honest.

chapters.title: Falsifiability
chapters.hook: The praise cards look convincing until Chris writes the result that would empty the shelf.
chapters.counterintuition: A claim that can explain every outcome has made itself weaker, not stronger; but real confidence starts when you name the observation that would make the claim lose.
chapters.tryThisNow: Take one belief you are using this week and complete this sentence: I will be wrong if I observe ____ by ____. Make the blank visible and dated.
chapters.keyTakeaway: A belief becomes usable when it risks a clear loss; write the disproof before collecting evidence that flatters it.

breakdown.fastRead:
Sample packets sit beside a clipboard of praise cards. Chris wants to believe the supplement reduces afternoon fatigue. The cards make that easy. Before he reads another glowing note, he writes the outcome that would make him pull the product from the front shelf.

That is falsifiability. A claim gets stronger when it exposes itself to a possible loss. If every outcome can be explained afterward, the claim has protected itself from learning.

Do not ask only what would support the idea. Ask what would kill it.
breakdown.deepRead:
Karl Popper's pressure point is simple: a claim that cannot lose has not earned a win. A useful claim forbids something from happening. It says, if I am right, this result should appear and that result should not. The forbidden result is what gives the claim weight.

Confirmation is cheap when you go shopping for it. A tired customer who felt better after a supplement, a visitor who praised evening museum hours, a swimmer who liked the sprint set: all of those can be real and still fail to test the claim. Support matters most when the claim first risked being wrong. Without a possible loss, the claim only learns how to survive.

Disproof gives the idea a spine.

Peter Cathcart Wason's experiments matter because the mind keeps reaching for the card that says yes when the useful card may say no. We like confirming cases because they feel cooperative. They let us keep the story. The harder move is to seek the case that would force a revision before pride attaches to the conclusion.

The limit is clear. Falsifiability is not a complete theory of truth. Some human questions are not clean experiments. But whenever a practical claim guides action, you can usually name a dated observation that would make you change course.
breakdown.fullRead:
Margaux stands under the museum atrium lights with the Friday-night ticket scanner blinking beside the overtime roster. She believes evening hours will bring younger visitors. The easy path is to run the pilot, collect kind comments, and call the energy a sign. Instead, before the first Friday opens, she writes the loss condition: if under-30 ticket scans fail to rise after four Fridays, the hypothesis loses.

That sentence changes the whole pilot. Staff are no longer hunting for anecdotes that keep the idea alive. They know what the claim must risk. The prediction is public enough to hurt and narrow enough to teach.

What would make your favorite idea embarrassing by next month?

Henrik faces the same discipline at the pool. Chlorine haze sits above lane four while the stopwatch clicks. He believes extra sprint sets improve starts. The swimmers feel worked, and the assistant likes the plan. Henrik still times three starts before the block, three starts after, and names the result that will end the new routine. Without that line, fatigue can masquerade as progress.

A flexible claim has a seductive quality. If museum attendance rises, the idea worked. If it falls, the marketing was weak. If it stays flat, the pilot needs more time. Every result gets absorbed. That kind of explanation feels resilient, but it is really insulated. It cannot learn because it cannot lose.

Popper treated that insulation as a serious defect. The point was not that every valuable idea belongs in a lab. The point was that a claim gains discipline when it permits reality to say no. Wason showed why this is difficult: people naturally look for the matching card, the agreeing case, the result that keeps the rule standing. Falsifiability asks you to turn around and inspect the card that could break it.

Kasia does this with a fundraising email. Two subject lines sit on sticky notes beside the unsubscribe column. The urgent line will probably lift open rates. She says the line must lose if unsubscribes pass a set threshold, even if opens climb. That protects the team from proving only the part of the idea they wanted to prove.

The practical version is blunt. A claim should leave a mark before the results arrive: a number, a date, a threshold, or a visible behavior that would make the team change course. Without that mark, the idea can keep moving the finish line and call every outcome support.

The practical version is blunt. Before the test begins, decide what would count against you. Make it measurable enough to act on. Make it close enough that you cannot postpone judgment forever. Then let the result touch the claim. You are not trying to embarrass yourself. You are trying to keep reality in the room early enough to matter.

A claim that risks nothing teaches nothing. A claim that can lose can also earn trust.

examples.title: Chris Writes the Pull Rule
examples.scenario: Sample packets sit beside a clipboard of praise cards at the front counter. Chris, the wellness retailer, wants the new supplement to reduce afternoon fatigue because customers keep leaving cheerful notes. Before he reads another testimonial, his pen hovers over the fatigue log. He must decide what result would make him pull the product from the shelf instead of searching for more support. The label stays on the bottle until one patient group can make the claim lose.
examples.whatToDo: Write the pull-from-shelf rule before counting praise cards. Define the fatigue-log result that would make the claim lose, then run the trial against that line.
examples.whyItMatters: Testimonials can confirm almost anything after the fact. A prewritten loss rule makes the supplement claim answer to a result that can actually hurt it.

examples.title: Margaux Sets the Four-Friday Threshold
examples.scenario: Will evening hours actually bring younger visitors, or just make the atrium feel livelier? Margaux watches the Friday-night ticket scanner blink beside the overtime roster. She predicts the under-30 scans will rise, then writes the four-Friday threshold that would prove her wrong. Before approving the pilot, she has to decide whether that loss condition is clear enough to stop the idea. The scanner report will matter more than praise gathered in the lobby after the event.
examples.whatToDo: Commit to the under-30 scan threshold before the pilot starts. If four Fridays miss it, stop treating atmosphere and compliments as proof.
examples.whyItMatters: The threshold turns a hopeful program into a risky prediction. Without it, every pleasant evening can be reinterpreted as success.

examples.title: Henrik Times the Starts Twice
examples.scenario: Chlorine haze hangs above lane four as Henrik, the coach, clicks the stopwatch for the third start. The assistant likes the new sprint block, and the swimmers look satisfyingly tired. Henrik writes the before times, then says which after-times would make them stop. He has to decide before practice ends whether exhaustion will count as effort or whether only faster starts can save the plan. The stopwatches decide the routine before tired swimmers can call effort progress.
examples.whatToDo: Measure starts before and after the sprint block, then obey the stopping rule. If the starts do not improve, remove the extra work instead of praising effort.
examples.whyItMatters: Fatigue can feel like evidence when the coach wants the plan to work. Timing the result gives the claim a possible loss.

examples.title: Kasia Protects Against Opens
examples.scenario: "The urgent line will win opens," the analyst says. Two subject lines sit on sticky notes beside the unsubscribe column. Kasia, the communications lead, nods and points to the loss rule. "If unsubscribes cross this level, it loses even with more opens." Before the send button lights up, she must decide whether the test is measuring attention or damaging trust. The unsubscribe threshold stays visible even if the open-rate graph looks exciting.
examples.whatToDo: Set the unsubscribe loss rule beside the open-rate goal. Let the subject line fail if it buys attention by burning donor trust.
examples.whyItMatters: A test that counts only the flattering metric protects the favored idea. A falsifying metric keeps the team from winning the wrong game.

examples.title: Devon Uses the Cutoff
examples.scenario: It took Devon, the seed cooperative manager, one greenhouse tray to learn whether the new drying process had been protected from failure. Pale seedlings lean toward the fan, and the germination cutoff is taped to the bench. The batch misses the line. Instead of blaming the cold week, Devon compares the tray to the rule he wrote before the test and records the process as failed for the spring run. The seed tray is split before the team starts explaining every sprout as proof.
examples.whatToDo: Use the cutoff written before the tray sprouted. Do not rescue the drying process with a weather story after the result is already visible.
examples.whyItMatters: A prewritten cutoff blocks after-the-fact flexibility. It keeps a costly seed process from surviving by inventing explanations after growers have lost time.

examples.title: Jack Separates Engagement From Learning
examples.scenario: You watch Jack spread laminated reading cards beside a tablet cart before the tutoring program opens. The game looks lively, and students ask for it during snack. Before launch, Jack writes the disproof rule: if cold-read summaries do not improve by week three, the tool is entertainment, not instruction. Three weeks later, he reads the summaries before the usage report. The tutoring promise now has a date when the claim either earns trust or gets revised.
examples.whatToDo: Judge the game by cold-read summaries, not by enthusiasm alone. Keep it only if the prewritten learning result improves by the deadline.
examples.whyItMatters: Engagement can confirm a tool that teaches little. The disproof rule protects students from losing weeks to something that only feels productive.

questions.prompt: A team is about to launch a new onboarding video and believes it will improve retention after the first month. Before launch, what would make the claim falsifiable?
choices: A clear result, named in advance, that would make them stop using the video.
A list of comments from new hires who liked the video.
A promise to review retention whenever the team has enough time.
questions.explanation: A falsifiable claim names the losing result before the evidence arrives. Positive comments support the idea weakly, and an undefined future review lets the claim keep moving.

questions.prompt: A manager of a busy cafe says a new pastry display increases morning sales, but she has only heard staff praise the look of the case. Which test best exposes the claim to possible disproof?
choices: Ask regulars whether the display looks better than the old one.
Track morning pastry sales for two weeks and predefine the sales lift required to keep the display.
Keep the display for a month because visual changes need time to work.
questions.explanation: The pre-set sales lift gives the claim a clear way to lose. Opinions about appearance and open-ended time both make it easier to protect the preferred story.

questions.prompt: A manager claims remote Fridays improve deep work. Productivity rises, but meeting load also falls that month. What should she do next?
choices: Declare the claim confirmed because the result moved in the right direction.
Ask employees which condition they enjoyed more.
Define what result would separate the Friday policy from the meeting reduction.
questions.explanation: The rise alone is not enough because another change may explain it. A sharper test must expose the specific remote-Friday claim to possible disproof.

questions.prompt: A museum pilot for evening hours gets kind visitor comments after opening night, but the under-30 ticket scans barely move. What should the team do?
choices: Keep the drill if players report that it feels demanding.
Replace the drill because intensity is too subjective to measure.
Name the performance result that must improve, and stop the drill if it does not.
questions.explanation: The drill needs a result that can defeat the coach's claim. Feeling intense can confirm the coach's preference without proving the drill improves performance.

questions.prompt: A product lead says every outcome from a pilot proves the idea: growth means demand, flat use means poor marketing, decline means users need more education. What is wrong?
choices: The claim cannot lose because every result is explained after the fact.
The claim is too negative about users to be tested fairly.
The pilot should have used more customer interviews before launch.
questions.explanation: The pilot has become self-protecting. Interviews may help, but the deeper flaw is that no possible result is allowed to count against the idea.

questions.prompt: A training program gets rave testimonials, but the prewritten loss condition says test scores must rise by Friday. What is the disciplined response?
choices: Collect more replies until the pattern is impossible to ignore.
Ask board members whether the email sounds persuasive.
Set a prewritten rule for donations and unsubscribes that would make the email fail.
questions.explanation: Grateful replies are easy confirmations. A rule covering donations and unsubscribes makes the claim risk a meaningful loss instead of counting only praise.

questions.prompt: A teacher believes a new app improves reading comprehension because students use it eagerly. Which evidence would most directly test the claim?
choices: Student quotes about whether the app feels fun.
A pre-set improvement in cold-read summaries by a specific week.
The number of minutes students spend inside the app.
questions.explanation: The claim is about comprehension, so the test must risk failure on comprehension. Fun and usage can be real while leaving the learning claim untested.

questions.prompt: A founder says a pricing change is good because revenue rose after it. Refunds also rose, and support tickets doubled. How should the claim be evaluated?
choices: Revenue is the cleanest signal, so the pricing claim is confirmed.
The claim should be tested against a prewritten package of results, including refunds and support load.
The price change should be reversed because any negative side effect disproves it.
questions.explanation: A narrow revenue metric can protect the favored claim. A prewritten result set gives the pricing idea a way to lose if it buys revenue through hidden damage.

questions.prompt: A manager says the new process must be working because every result can be explained afterward as part of the plan. What is the strongest critique?
choices: Ask nurses whether the checklist feels clearer than the old process.
Use the checklist for a month and discuss any complaints afterward.
Define the next-day patient answers that must improve, collect them, and retire the checklist if they do not.
questions.explanation: The design names the result that can defeat the checklist. Staff impressions and vague later discussion keep the claim too flexible to teach much.

reviewCards.front: You believe a change worked because you can find several confirming examples. What should you retrieve?
reviewCards.back: Confirmations are easy to collect. A stronger claim names the result that would make it wrong before it starts gathering evidence.

reviewCards.front: A favorite idea explains every possible outcome after the fact. What is the warning?
reviewCards.back: The idea has protected itself from disproof. If no result can count against it, the flexibility is weakness, not strength.

reviewCards.front: Before running a pilot, what sentence makes the claim safer to trust later?
reviewCards.back: Write: I will be wrong if I observe a specific result by a specific time. That sentence gives reality permission to defeat the claim.

reviewCards.front: Why do risky predictions count for more than easy confirmations?
reviewCards.back: A risky prediction exposes the idea to a real loss. Easy confirmations can be selected after the fact and may only show that you looked for support.

reviewCards.front: A team wants support before it has named a losing result. What practical move should you retrieve?
reviewCards.back: It protects the decision from confirmation bias. You learn faster because the test is aimed at the place where the belief could break.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: You learn to make beliefs risk a visible loss. The skill is writing the disconfirming result before pride, sunk cost, or public commitment makes the idea hard to kill.

ifThenPlans.plan: If you propose a pilot, then write the exact metric and deadline that would make you stop it before the pilot begins.
If you claim a routine is helping, then name the observable result that must improve and the date when you will check it.
If people keep trading supporting anecdotes, then ask each side what result would make its claim wrong.
If a theory explains every possible result, then narrow it until at least one result would count against it.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Take one belief guiding a real action and write the sentence: I will be wrong if I observe ____ by ____. Put it where you will see it before acting.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Each week, review one decision you supported strongly. Record the confirming evidence you noticed, the disconfirming evidence you looked for, and whether the claim had a real way to lose.

memorableLines.text: Disproof gives the idea a spine.
A flexible claim has a seductive quality.
A claim that risks nothing teaches nothing.

chapters.title: First Principles Thinking
chapters.hook: The yellow maintenance cart looks expensive only while the bid stays bundled.
chapters.counterintuition: Analogy is not wrong, but it becomes dangerous when the old shape hides facts that first principles thinking needs to take apart.
chapters.tryThisNow: Write one problem as two columns: facts I can verify and assumptions I inherited. Rebuild one possible move using only the verified column.
chapters.keyTakeaway: First principles thinking breaks a problem into verified facts, then rebuilds from those facts instead of copying the nearest familiar solution.

breakdown.fastRead:
A yellow maintenance cart sits beside a stack of vendor bids. Matthew has been told electric carts are too expensive, and every quote seems to prove it. Then he separates battery cells, frame, charger, and service contract on the bid sheet. The bundled price stops looking like a law.

First principles thinking begins when you pull apart the package. Which parts are facts? Which parts are conventions, assumptions, or copied designs? Reasoning by analogy asks what similar buyers usually do. First principles asks what must be true here.

Take it apart before you improve it.
breakdown.deepRead:
Elon Musk's useful move was not optimism; it was asking what the materials and physics cost before accepting the market's price tag. That is the discipline. A price, process, or design often arrives as a finished object. It feels solid because other people have accepted it. First principles thinking loosens the screws.

The Lego house example works because the house stops being a house when the bricks come loose, and that is exactly when new designs become possible. You cannot rebuild while the old arrangement still has authority. Once the pieces are separate, you can ask what each one actually does.

Disassembly creates room for facts that habit covered.

Juliette sees it in the bakery. Butter flakes stick to the inside of a collapsed pastry box. Buying a thicker version of the same box would copy the old assumption. Instead, she takes the box apart and writes what the croissant actually needs: steam escape, corner protection, and room for flakes to fall without soaking the pastry. The new package comes from the pastry, not from the old box.

The limit matters. First principles do not mean ignoring expertise. They mean refusing to treat habit as proof. Good analogies can save time when the situation is stable and well understood. The danger appears when analogy smuggles in assumptions that no one has checked.
breakdown.fullRead:
Lars hears a cart wheel squeak outside room 417 and watches the industry benchmark fall apart. The competitor target says one attendant can turn a certain number of rooms per shift. His hotel has tighter elevators, heavier bedding, and a safety checklist competitors do not use. So he walks one reset with a timer, breaks the job into physical tasks, and rebuilds the staffing model from linen weight, bathroom steps, inspection time, and elevator waits.

That is the quiet version of first principles. No speech about disruption. No thrill of being original. Just a refusal to let a borrowed number do work it has not earned. The borrowed number may still be useful later, but only after the local facts have had their turn.

What part of your current problem is a fact, and what part is furniture someone else arranged?

The repeated why is not a child's habit here; it is a shovel. Socratic questioning and the Five Whys both work by digging under the first answer. Why are missed appointments rising? Because patients forget. Why do they forget? Because reminder texts go out during shifts. Why does that matter? Because many patients cannot answer phones at work and need bus timing more than memory. Hadiya stops shopping for reminder software and starts redesigning around shift work and transit.

The method is hard because assumptions rarely announce themselves. They sound like reality. Batteries cost this much. Boxes look like this. A room reset takes that long. Patients miss visits because they forget. A robot chassis should copy last year's winner. First principles thinking slows you down long enough to ask whether those sentences are facts or just inherited arrangements.

Chiara shows the younger version at the robotics table. Aluminum brackets scatter across a plywood bridge mockup while the team copies the winning chassis from last year. She asks what the robot must actually cross, carry, and turn around. Three copied parts come off the table. The terrain rule sheet, not the old trophy photo, becomes the design authority.

There is a cost. Taking things apart can waste time when the existing pattern is already well tested. It can also tempt people into blank-slate arrogance, where every inherited practice is treated as stupidity. That is not the move. The move is to separate the useful inherited pieces from the unexamined ones.

Use analogy when it still fits. Use first principles when the old shape is expensive, confusing, or blocking better options. The signal is friction: a borrowed number that keeps failing, a copied design that keeps breaking, or a price that no one can explain from its parts.

Once the problem is apart, rebuild from verified ground. The result may look ordinary. It may look strange. Either way, it belongs to the facts in front of you, not to the first example your memory handed you.

examples.title: Matthew Unbundles the Cart Bid
examples.scenario: Matthew, the facilities manager, parks a yellow maintenance cart beside a stack of vendor bids in the garage. The battery pack quote looks like a single fixed price, but he must decide whether to accept it or break the cart into cells, casing, charger, labor, and disposal. The parts list reveals which costs are physics and which are vendor packaging.
examples.whatToDo: Break the bid into parts before rejecting the option. Price the cells, frame, charger, and service contract separately, then rebuild the comparison from verified costs.
examples.whyItMatters: The bundled price imports the vendor's assumptions. Separating the pieces lets Matthew see which cost is real and which one belongs to the package design.

examples.title: Juliette Rebuilds Around Steam
examples.scenario: Butter flakes stick to the inside of a collapsed pastry box after the lunch delivery run. Juliette, the bakery manager, first orders thicker samples, then stops. She cuts the crushed box open, lists steam escape, corner pressure, and flake space, and designs from those needs instead of copying the old shape. The next test box looks less pretty and carries the croissant intact. The new insert is sketched beside the old box so the team can see which assumptions survived disassembly.
examples.whatToDo: Stop improving the old box. List what the pastry physically needs, then rebuild the package from steam, pressure, and movement.
examples.whyItMatters: A thicker bad design preserves the hidden assumption. First principles shift authority from the old package to the croissant's actual constraints.

examples.title: Lars Times the Room Reset
examples.scenario: It took Lars, the operations analyst, one squeaking cart outside room 417 to distrust the competitor benchmark. The industry target said the shift was staffed correctly, but attendants were skipping safety checks. Lars walks one reset with a timer, counts linen weight, bathroom steps, elevator waits, and inspection time, then rebuilds the staffing model from the tasks the benchmark never saw. His stopwatch separates linen weight, elevator wait, and inspection time before the benchmark gets another vote.
examples.whatToDo: Take the benchmark apart into the physical work it hides. Time the actual reset and rebuild the staffing target from the room's real tasks.
examples.whyItMatters: The benchmark is analogy, not ground truth. It may fit another hotel while failing the constraints of this building and checklist.

examples.title: Chiara Removes Three Brackets
examples.scenario: "Last year's chassis won," one student says as aluminum brackets scatter across the plywood bridge mockup. Chiara, the robotics mentor, opens the terrain rule sheet and asks what the robot must cross, carry, and turn around. Three copied parts come off the table. Before the build night ends, she must decide whether the trophy photo or the terrain rules get to define the robot. The terrain rule sheet sits in the center of the table, replacing the trophy photo as the authority.
examples.whatToDo: Start from the terrain requirement, payload, and turning space. Remove copied parts that do not serve those facts before the team cuts more metal.
examples.whyItMatters: The old chassis is an analogy from a different problem. Taking it apart lets the team design for the constraints in front of them.

examples.title: Hadiya Digs Under Forgetfulness
examples.scenario: Why did the reminder text fail if the patient received it? Hadiya, the clinic manager, sits with a missed-visit log, an unanswered text, and a bus schedule printout. Five whys later, forgetfulness has disappeared as the main constraint. Shift work and a bad bus connection are doing the damage. Before buying reminder software, she must decide whether memory is really the problem. The bus timetable and shift calendar now sit beside the reminder script before anyone buys new software.
examples.whatToDo: Run the Five Whys on one missed visit before buying software. Rebuild the fix around shift timing and transit instead of copying a reminder-tool answer.
examples.whyItMatters: The first explanation was an assumption dressed as fact. Digging below it changes the problem from memory to access.

examples.title: Pavel Lists the Stage Constraints
examples.scenario: You watch Pavel, the volunteer technical director, stand in the community theater aisle while dust brightens inside a stage beam above a coil of old cable. The donated lights look modern. The building's electrical limit does not. Pavel lists electricity, throw distance, heat, and cue needs before deciding which fixtures help and which only look like theater gear he recognizes. The lighting cue list is rebuilt from sightline, cable run, and load limit instead of last year's rig.
examples.whatToDo: Judge the lights from the stage constraints: power, throw distance, heat, and cues. Accept only the donated gear that fits those facts.
examples.whyItMatters: Familiar equipment can smuggle in the wrong assumptions. The stage's physical limits, not the donation's appeal, should shape the rig.

questions.prompt: A city buyer rejects electric carts because every vendor bundle is expensive. What first-principles move should come before the rejection?
choices: Compare the bundle with what other cities bought last year.
Ask staff whether they prefer gas or electric carts.
Break the cart into battery, frame, charger, and service costs.
questions.explanation: The bundle may hide assumptions. Separating the cart into parts lets the buyer reason from verified costs rather than a vendor's packaged answer.

questions.prompt: A bakery's delivery boxes crush croissants. The supplier suggests thicker versions of the same box. Which response best applies first principles?
choices: List what the croissant needs during delivery, then design from those physical needs.
Buy the thickest available box because stronger materials usually solve crushing.
Ask competitors which pastry boxes they use for similar deliveries.
questions.explanation: The croissant's constraints are the foundation. Thicker boxes and competitor choices may preserve the old assumption instead of rebuilding from steam, pressure, and movement.

questions.prompt: An analyst copies a competitor's hotel staffing benchmark, then learns attendants are skipping safety checks. What did the analogy hide?
choices: The competitor may have better staff morale.
The benchmark may not include this hotel's actual room-reset tasks and constraints.
Safety checks are probably too detailed for daily operations.
questions.explanation: The copied benchmark compressed a different setting. First principles require breaking the work into tasks before accepting a borrowed room-per-attendant number.

questions.prompt: A robotics team wants to copy last year's winning chassis, but the new contest requires a bridge crossing and tight turn. Which move is strongest?
choices: Copy the chassis because prior victory is evidence of good design.
Start from the bridge, payload, and turn radius before deciding which old parts belong.
Avoid all old parts because first principles require a completely new design.
questions.explanation: The new terrain facts should govern the design. First principles do not ban old parts; they make every part earn its place against the current constraints.

questions.prompt: A clinic blames missed appointments on forgetfulness and buys reminder software. A Five Whys pass shows patients receive texts during shifts and miss the bus afterward. What changes?
choices: The clinic should send more reminders to overcome the work-shift problem.
The problem shifts from memory to access, so the fix must be rebuilt around timing and transit.
The clinic should stop using texts because patients cannot answer during work.
questions.explanation: The first explanation was an assumption. Digging down revealed a different constraint, so copying the reminder-software answer would solve the wrong problem.

questions.prompt: A theater receives donated lights that look professional, but the building has old wiring and a shallow stage. Which plan best fits the model?
choices: Use the donated lights because professional gear raises production quality.
Reject the donation because old buildings cannot handle modern lighting.
List power, heat, throw distance, and cue needs, then keep only fixtures that fit.
questions.explanation: The stage constraints are the ground facts. The donation's professional look is only analogy unless the lights fit power, heat, distance, and cue requirements.

questions.prompt: A restaurant team says delivery boxes should just be thicker because the old box collapsed, but nobody has listed steam, corner impact, and flake space. What should they do first?
choices: Which competitor copied the model first?
What must be true about our costs, customers, and risk for this pricing to work here?
How can we make the same pricing look more original?
questions.explanation: The question separates local facts from inherited analogy. Competitor history and cosmetic originality both keep the old structure in charge.

questions.prompt: A clinic blames missed visits on memory and wants reminder software, but patient shifts and bus timing may be the real constraints. Which question is strongest?
choices: Stop asking and rebuild the option around the verified constraint.
Keep asking why until a person can be held responsible.
Return to the original process because too much analysis slows action.
questions.explanation: First principles are meant to guide rebuilding. Once a verified constraint appears, the next move is design from it, not endless questioning or blame.

questions.prompt: A robotics club copies last year's winning chassis, but this year's bridge rules change the turning radius and load. What should the team do?
choices: The template is familiar and easy to defend to leadership.
The team wants to feel more innovative than competitors.
The old template is expensive and rests on assumptions that no longer match the problem.
questions.explanation: First principles are most valuable when the inherited shape is costly or mismatched. Familiarity and innovation theater are both weak reasons for the harder path.

reviewCards.front: A solution arrives as a finished bundle. What should you retrieve before accepting it?
reviewCards.back: Take the bundle apart. Separate verified facts from inherited assumptions, then rebuild from the facts that actually govern the problem.

reviewCards.front: A team says, This is how everyone in our industry does it. What is the first-principles question?
reviewCards.back: Ask what must be true here. Industry analogy may be useful, but it should not smuggle in assumptions that no longer match local constraints.

reviewCards.front: Why does disassembling a problem create new options?
reviewCards.back: The old arrangement loses authority when the pieces come apart. You can then recombine verified pieces instead of improving the inherited shape.

reviewCards.front: How do the Five Whys help without becoming endless analysis?
reviewCards.back: They dig below the first explanation until a real constraint appears. Once it appears, the next step is rebuilding around it, not asking forever.

reviewCards.front: When should analogy still be used?
reviewCards.back: Use analogy when the situation is stable and the borrowed pattern still fits. Shift to first principles when the pattern is costly, stale, or mismatched.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: You learn to take inherited answers apart before improving them. The skill is to separate verified facts from assumptions, then rebuild one option from what the problem itself requires.

ifThenPlans.plan: If a quote arrives as one bundled number, then separate materials, labor, service, and risk before accepting the price.
If a benchmark feels convenient, then walk the real work once and list the tasks the benchmark may hide.
If the team wants to copy a competitor, then write the facts that make your users, costs, or constraints different.
If the first explanation feels too easy, then ask why until you reach a constraint you can verify or act on.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Choose one annoying problem and make two columns: verified facts and inherited assumptions. Build one next action using only the verified facts column.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once a week, take one repeated process and disassemble it into parts. Mark which parts are facts, which are habits, and which assumptions deserve a small test.

memorableLines.text: Take it apart before you improve it.
Disassembly creates room for facts that habit covered.
The method is hard because assumptions rarely announce themselves.

chapters.title: Thought Experiment
chapters.hook: Three blank case cards under a harsh lamp reveal the rule before any real patient is waiting.
chapters.counterintuition: Imagination is not useful because it is unconstrained, but because a strong thought experiment fixes the rules and lets the hidden consequence appear early.
chapters.tryThisNow: Choose one risky action. Run it once in your head with one fixed constraint, then write the first hidden assumption that appears.
chapters.keyTakeaway: A thought experiment is structured imagination: simplify the scene, fix the constraint, and inspect the consequence before reality makes it expensive.

breakdown.fastRead:
Three blank case cards sit under a harsh meeting-room lamp. Ryan removes every patient name before the ethics board chooses scarce-bed criteria. No ambulance is waiting. No family is crying outside the door. The board has to expose its rule before a real crisis forces the rule onto a person.

That is a thought experiment. It is not daydreaming. It is a mental simulation with constraints tight enough to teach. You simplify reality on purpose so one hidden assumption or consequence can show itself.

Run the future while the cost is still imaginary.
breakdown.deepRead:
Ernst Mach's point gives imagination a job: spend a few minutes in the mind before spending money in the world. A thought experiment is a low-cost test bed. It lets you explore what is costly, impossible, dangerous, or not ready for physical trial.

Einstein belongs here as a reminder that the best mental simulation is not loose fantasy; it is imagination held inside rules. The rules are what make the exercise useful. If anything can happen, nothing can be learned. If the conditions are fixed, the mind can trace implications.

The constraint does the teaching.

Manon uses this at the satellite console. A red sensor flag blinks over the launch-window countdown. Instead of asking whether the team feels ready, she asks them to simulate launch with the sensor fault unresolved and name the first irreversible loss. The vote changes because the mental run exposes what optimism had skipped.

A good simulation also says what has been removed. Ryan strips names from triage cases to test criteria, not to pretend patients are blank cards. Tomas adds rain to the festival plan to reveal crowd flow, not to predict every storm. The simplification is a tool, and tools have edges.

The limit is just as important. A thought experiment can reveal assumptions; it cannot certify the world. Once the real test becomes possible and safe, reality gets the final say.
breakdown.fullRead:
Rainwater pools in the chalk marks for the ticket line. Tomas, the festival organizer, is deciding whether rain-or-shine really means rain-or-shine. He walks the whole festival in his head during a thunderstorm: vendor coolers under thin tents, customers crowding under the brewery awning, parents with strollers stopped at the narrow ticket gate. The simulation is simple, but it is not vague. Weather, crowd flow, and the ticket queue stay fixed.

By the end, he moves the queue before the first drop falls.

What constraint would make your plan reveal its weak point in ninety seconds?

The trolley problem lineage lasts because a stripped-down scene can make a hidden moral rule show itself. You do not need a full city, a full history, or every emotional detail to learn something. The simplification is the instrument. It removes enough reality for the rule to become visible. Then, if the situation is real, you bring the missing reality back before acting.

Anke does that with discharge paperwork. You watch her pretend to be a tired patient with one bus transfer, a plastic pharmacy bag, and a phone number card buried under two pages of instructions. The packet looks clear from the nurse's station. In the simulation, it fails at the bus stop. The medication list is too dense, the callback number is too hidden, and the packet assumes calm attention the patient will not have.

A weak thought experiment is just a story that protects the preferred answer. A strong one makes the answer work under fixed pressure. It says: keep the launch fault in place; remove the patient names; add rain; make the patient tired; cut the fuel cache by ten percent. Then watch what breaks.

Akira writes the future postmortem from the arctic field camp before the team flies. Frost sits on the fuel drum stencil, and the imagined report says the generator ran short on day nine. That invented failure exposes the hidden assumption: the plan used ideal generator hours, not storm-bound hours. The fuel cache changes before anyone is cold.

Isabel's audition rule shows the softer version. Numbered cards fan beside a piano bench, and the screen hides the performer's face. When she mentally walks the day from hallway to sign-in desk to screen, accompanist access still reveals advantage. The rule had solved one visible bias while leaving another path open. The mental walk found the leak before the audition season began.

Thought experiments are powerful because ideas are cheap to move. They are dangerous when their tidiness becomes a substitute for evidence. Use them to find the assumption, the implication, the moral rule, or the failure path. Then, when the world can answer safely, let it answer.

The mind is a rehearsal room, not the whole stage.

examples.title: Ryan Removes the Names
examples.scenario: Three blank case cards sit under a harsh meeting-room lamp before Tuesday's ethics board. Ryan, the hospital chair, has removed every patient name from the scarce-bed exercise. The protocol draft lists stated criteria, but the board keeps drifting toward personal sympathy. Before any real patient is waiting, Ryan must decide whether they will choose by the written rule or by the story each card used to carry.
